title: The China spiral
hook: In ten days of April 2025 the US and China raised tariffs on each other to 145% and 125%. How the spiral started, how it was unwound, and what rare earths had to do with it.
notes: US tariffs on China: executive orders 14195, 14228, 14257, 14259, 14266, 14298, 14334, 14357, 14358 and 14389, Proclamation 11012 and USTR notice 2026-15181 (Federal Register). Only tariffs introduced since 2025 are counted; the Section 301 tariffs of 2018–19 (7.5–25% on about two-thirds of imports from China, up to 100% on some goods since 2024) and Section 232 sector tariffs apply on top. China's tariffs on US goods: announcements of the State Council Tariff Commission (April and May 2025; 2025 No. 9 and No. 10 of 5 November 2025). China's line stops on 20 February 2026: we found no official notice changing its 10% after the US Supreme Court ruling, so its later level is not shown. Rare earths: MOFCOM and customs announcement 2025 No. 18 (4 April 2025); MOFCOM announcements 2025 No. 61 and 62 (9 October 2025), suspended until 10 November 2026 by announcement No. 70 (7 November 2025). Summit outcomes: White House fact sheets and MOFCOM statements, which differ in places (for example on farm purchases and rare earths). The September 2026 extension of the truce to 10 January 2027 was announced by US Treasury Secretary Bessent; China had not confirmed it in the sources checked. Trade values: US Census Bureau, 2024.

scenes.title: The biggest imbalance
scenes.text: In 2024 the US bought about $440 billion of goods from China and sold it about $143 billion. No other country's trade with the US was so lopsided in dollars. The first tariffs of Trump's second term, ordered on 1 February 2025, targeted China, Canada and Mexico; only China's escalated into triple digits.

routes.label: $440 bn of goods to the US

scenes.title: It starts with fentanyl
scenes.text: On 4 February 2025 the US added 10% to all goods from China, Hong Kong and Macau, citing the flow of fentanyl. A month later it doubled the rate to 20%. China answered with targeted tariffs of 10–15% on US coal, gas, oil, farm machinery, cars and then farm goods, but not yet on everything.

captions.20250304: US: +20%. China targets US farm goods from 10 March.

scenes.title: Ten days in April
scenes.text: The 2 April 'reciprocal' tariffs put another 34% on China. Beijing matched it with 34% on all US goods; Washington raised its rate to 84%, then 125%; Beijing followed to 84% and 125%. By 12 April Chinese goods paid 145% in new US tariffs and US goods 125% in China. Shipments between the two largest economies plunged.

scenes.title: China's other weapon
scenes.text: On 4 April 2025 China also required export licences for seven rare earths, including dysprosium and terbium, which go into magnets for cars, wind turbines and weapons. China mines most of the world's rare earths and refines nearly all heavy ones. Shipments slumped and some carmakers outside China halted lines. In October China widened the rules to foreign products with traces of Chinese rare earths.

scenes.title: Truce in Geneva, deal in Busan
scenes.text: After talks in Geneva, both sides cut their rates on 14 May 2025: the US to 30%, China to 10%, suspending the rest for 90 days. At a meeting in Busan on 30 October, Presidents Trump and Xi agreed a one-year truce: the US halved its fentanyl tariff, for 20% in total, and China paused its October rare-earth rules for a year, dropped its farm tariffs and resumed soybean purchases.

scenes.title: After the court
scenes.text: When the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs in February 2026, the 20% on Chinese goods gave way to a 10% surcharge, and from 24 July to a 12.5% 'forced labour' tariff, on top of the older tariffs from 2018. Trump visited Beijing in May 2026; the sides agreed a 'Board of Trade' to negotiate tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods each way. In September, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said the truce would run to 10 January 2027; China had not confirmed it.
